raw_response.country: Multiple low- and lower-middle-income countries across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Pacific (including Bangladesh, Benin, Bolivia, Cambodia, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Peru, Rwanda, Senegal, Tanzania, Timor-Leste, Uganda, and Vietnam)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines water and sanitation service access for poor urban and rural households and communities in low- and lower-middle-income countries.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, though borderline in scope breadth. Under the plain wording, the review clearly examines institutional, governance, policy, and regulatory factors (private and social enterprise roles, public-private partnerships, civil society interfaces, decentralisation, and regulation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, substantial portions of the review cover sanitation marketing, supply-chain viability, and CSO capacity building (which alone would be out-of-scope commercial/behavioural promotion or project delivery), but the review also explicitly synthesizes empirical evidence on multiple rule-type mechanisms directly governing poor households' service access: (1) provider ownership, contracting, and regulatory structures (for-profit private operators vs. social enterprises, rural piped-water PPPs, municipal-utility delegated management models, legalisation/formalisation of informal providers, licensing/taxes, accreditation, neighbourhood regulatory decentralisation, and enforcement fines on illegal dumping); (2) tariff, connection-fee, cost-recovery, and subsidy rules (high connection fees preventing poor households from connecting or locking them in, cost-recovery water tariffs pricing out poor rural households, and hardware/community or output-based connection subsidies); and (3) pricing discretion/accommodation (flexible pricing structures and instalment/credit payment schemes for poor customers).
criterion_notes.c3: Systematic empirical synthesis following ODI/DFID systematic review methodology: defined search strategy across databases, websites, journals, and sector networks (4,211 initial records screened to 164 mapped documents and 82 reviewed in detail), explicit inclusion criteria, structured rigour appraisal, and qualitative synthesis of predominantly primary empirical studies. Criterion 3 explicitly includes a systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports synthesized outcomes directly relevant to poor households' access, connection, affordability, and exclusion, including non-prioritisation of poor customers by profit-seeking operators, inability to afford connection fees or rural water tariffs leading poor households to rely on unsafe alternative water supplies, customer lock-in from high connection fees, and improved poor access under delegated management models or flexible pricing/instalment arrangements.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (poor households/communities and small-scale WASH enterprises in LMICs; unit of analysis: synthesis of 164 mapped / 82 detailed studies covering household/community access and enterprise-level operations), exposure (private/social enterprise delivery and ownership models, PPP/delegated management contracting, formalisation/regulation, and tariff/connection-fee/subsidy rules), outcome (household WASH access, affordability, and exclusion), and study design (systematic review / qualitative empirical synthesis) are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Micro, small and medium private and social enterprises are emerging as important players in the water, sanitation and hygiene sector. This paper provides a systematic review of literature on this topic. It assesses the current evidence base in three areas: factors affecting success of enterprise engagement; outcomes for the poor as a result of enterprise engagement; and lastly, how civil society organisations are engaging to support enterprise development.
The dominant type of study was found to be ‘primary empirical work’ with many such studies demonstrating strong rigour (see Figure 2).

‘Legalization of the informal market and decentralization of certain regulatory activities to the neighbourhood level are important steps in the efforts to improve service delivery to the urban poor’.
Evidence suggests that outcomes for poor households who cannot afford connections or the water tariffs include drawing on unsafe alternative water supplies

Delegated management models, where small-scale operators are contracted by municipal water utilities, have shown to provide an approach to allow access to water (and sanitation) services for the urban poor

raw_response.exposure: Private and social enterprise WASH service-delivery and ownership models (small-scale private operators, social enterprises, rural PPPs, municipal delegated management models, formalised vs. informal providers) and associated tariff, connection-fee, cost-recovery, subsidy, and regulatory mechanisms
raw_response.outcome: Household and community water and sanitation access and affordability for the poor (customer inclusion vs. exclusion/non-prioritisation, ability to afford connection fees and tariffs, customer lock-in, reliance on unsafe alternative water supplies), alongside enterprise business viability
raw_response.population_and_sample: Poor urban and rural households and communities, alongside micro, small, and medium private and social WASH enterprises/operators in low- and lower-middle-income countries; systematic review mapping 164 documents (from 4,211 search hits) and synthesizing 82 documents in detail (2008-2013)
raw_response.rationale: This 2014 paper matches the record metadata and is a full-text systematic empirical synthesis (eligible under Criterion 3) examining private and social enterprise roles in water and sanitation services for the poor across low- and lower-middle-income countries. Although a substantial share of the reviewed literature concerns enterprise viability, sanitation marketing, and CSO capacity building, the review explicitly synthesizes empirical evidence on rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification: private/social operator ownership, rural water PPPs, and municipal-utility delegated management models; formalisation, licensing, accreditation, and neighbourhood-level regulation of informal providers; and connection fees, cost-recovery tariffs, flexible/instalment pricing accommodations, and subsidies directly governing poor households' water and sanitation access, affordability, and exclusion. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are met for systematic-review inclusion (noting Criterion 6 is a quantitative-synthesis gate, not a review-eligibility gate). Confidence is rated medium because the review blends in-scope ownership, regulatory, and tariff/connection-fee mechanisms with broader sanitation-marketing and supply-chain enterprise themes.
raw_response.study_design: Systematic review (qualitative thematic synthesis of 164 mapped and 82 reviewed academic and grey literature documents, predominantly primary empirical studies)
